job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Zane Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Zane. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say is confidential. So you can give me the public view and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in power systems at Stonebridge, which is about how electricity gets from the plant to your kettle. I live at my uncle's place near the campus, pay a small rent and help with the garden. Mornings I'm in lectures, afternoons in the library, and Sundays are church and then lunch with the whole family. It's a quiet life and I like it quiet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study before, and how did it go?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Electrical engineering, a pass. I wasn't the sharpest in the exams, I'm better with a meter in my hand than a formula on a board. My dad runs a small electrical contracting firm in Pine Ridge, and I worked there on weekends, but that doesn't count as an internship on paper. No one else would take me for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, sensible, that's what I thought. People get carried away with new gadgets and then life carries on as it always did. I'd tell my cousins that a good trade still matters more than a good gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I still need to find work the ordinary way. There are jobs in power and installation near here, and I'd have a fair chance. The master's is mostly to please myself and to show I'm serious, and it costs more than I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course and apply to the grid company and two of the big installers, and I'd ask Dad to put in a word with the people he buys from. If nothing comes, I'd go into Dad's firm for a year, and I'd be happy enough there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. It's the world I understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it cost, that you don't like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 7,000 in loan so far, with a bit more next year. I don't like owing, my father taught me never to carry debt you can avoid. I've got a couple of months saved, and I'd keep that for emergencies, not for being proud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be happy in your father's firm. Is that a first choice or a fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. I want to prove I can get in on my own merit first. I'd like the grid company to hire me because I'm good, and not because my dad knows a man who buys cable from the same supplier.

I'd tell my cousins that life **carries on** as it always did.

The master's costs more than I like, with about **7,000** owed.
do: **Apply** to the grid company and two large installers.
Ask **Dad** to put in a word with his suppliers.
Join Dad's **firm** for a year if nothing comes.
feel: **Settled**; this is the world I understand.

steps.text: Apply to the grid company and two big installers

Work a year in Dad's firm if no offer comes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not all bad, but it's not all good either. If the paperwork and planning go to machines, the people who can actually wire a building still matter. I'd tell my cousins to learn a trade and not sit all day at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it unsettles me. The design side of power work is half the job I trained for, and software would eat that first. I've never used these tools and I'm not keen. I'd feel like the last one in the room to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean toward the installation and maintenance side, with real cables and switchgear. I'd do the apprenticeship-style route if a firm offers one, and I'd take a short course on the design software that firms use. I'd still hold off on the chatbots unless an employer says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary. Like when the weather changes and you can't say how bad it'll get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hold off on the chatbots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like asking a machine for an answer I can't test. In electrical work a wrong number can start a fire. If I can't prove a figure myself, I won't put it on a drawing that goes in a family's home. That's my rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a firm I respect showed me it checks out, with proper records, I'd try. Dad's old friend Mr Ferris says some firms now use them for quotes. If it's proven, I can learn. I just won't be first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, plain and simple. Families and churches and councils need time to catch up, and two years is nothing. I'd say we should look after our own, our families and neighbours, because nobody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm afraid. I'd have a master's and a pass degree in a field where the thinking half goes first. I'm not clever with the new tools and I'd have no time to become so. I'd be holding on to the hands-on half and hoping it lasts three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the job hunt for engineering offices and go straight into Dad's firm full time. I'd live at my uncle's, spend nothing I don't have to, and keep paying the loan. I'd also help at church with the food collection, because I think we'll need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid, and a bit ashamed. I don't like feeling that I can't do anything about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ashamed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my father built something with his hands and I went and borrowed money to study theory. I feel I spent my family's trust on a degree that a computer program may undo before I've used it. He would never say that, but I think it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the firm look like in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The jobs on site are still done by people for a few years. The quotes and paperwork, Dad's wife does them in the evening, and that goes to software first. I'd try to take that off her plate, and learn the program whether I like it or not.

say: Two years is **too fast**; families and councils need time.
We should look after our own, **families and neighbours**.

**Help** at church with the food collection.
feel: **Afraid** and a bit ashamed that I can't change it.

fieldNote: His traditional values push him toward **family** and church support.
Shame about debt and **theory** is the emotional core.
Plans to learn the quoting software despite his **dislike** of it.

steps.text: Join Dad's contracting firm full time and take over the quotes
Keep living at the uncle's house and cut all extra spending
Volunteer at the church food collection every week
Keep paying the loan every month from the firm's wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something you can work with. I'd tell people it's time to get the family finances in order, learn a useful trade, and not take on debt for things you don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's less frightening. I'd have a first job and some years of experience before it lands. I'd have paid down a good part of my loan. Hands-on work gets three more years, and that matters for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job with an installer or the grid company and work on site. I'd put away 200 a month and clear the loan. And I'd learn the basics of the design software, and maybe one AI tool, though only if my employer wants it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Manageable. There's a heaviness, but I can see a way through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'a way through' look like in numbers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two hundred a month saved, the loan down to nothing in about four years, and a spare room at my uncle's until then. It isn't fancy. A plan that's boring and paid for beats a plan that's clever and borrowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the roles on site are also taken sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to Dad's firm and we'd tighten our belts together. The firm's small enough that we'd see it coming. A small firm can turn faster than a big one, I think.

say: Five years is something you can **work with**.
Get the family **finances** in order and avoid debt you don't need.
think: I'd have a first job and a **good part** of my loan paid.
Hands-on work gets **three more years**, which matters for me.
do: **Take** a job with an installer or the grid company on site.
**Put away** 200 a month and clear the loan.

feel: **Manageable**: a heaviness, but I can see a way through.
S3.quote: A plan that's boring and paid for beats a plan that's clever and borrowed.
fieldNote: Time suits his **steady, cautious** instincts, with a plain money plan.

steps.text: Take an on-site job with an installer or the grid company
Save 200 a month and clear the loan in four years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and a man can build a whole life in that. I'd tell my cousins to marry well, work hard and keep their family close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly at ease. By 34 I could have a steady job, a house maybe, and children. Robots for hands-on work would come around 2039, and by then I'd be well into my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first engineering job, work toward a chartered qualification, and buy a house with a deposit saved over a few years. I'd keep helping at church. And I'd pick up the new tools gradually, once the older engineers at work show me they're safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the one where I can picture ordinary things like a kitchen table and children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there something about children in your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a couple, in time. A secure job and a house come first. I won't start a family on borrowed money, so the loan has to be gone before I ask anyone to marry me. That's the order for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a long timeline have any downside for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might make me lazy about learning. I'm already slow to pick up new things. Someone, perhaps my uncle or a colleague, would need to nudge me every year.

say: Ten years is long enough to build a **whole life**.
Work hard, marry well and keep **family** close.
think: By 34 I could have a steady job, a **house** and children.
Robots reach hands-on work around **2039**, well into my career.
do: **Take** the first engineering job and work toward chartered status.
**Save** over a few years for a house deposit.
Pick up the **new tools** gradually when colleagues show they're safe.
feel: **Calm**: I can picture a kitchen table and children.
S4.quote: I won't start a family on borrowed money, so the loan has to be gone before I ask anyone to marry me.
fieldNote: A long window suits his **traditional** life plan of work, house, family.
Money order is clear: **debt-free** before marriage.
Admits he needs **nudging** to keep learning.

steps.text: Take the first engineering job and work toward chartered status
Join the engineers' institution and start the chartered pathway

Clear the loan before planning a wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'm slow to change, and two years leaves no room to be slow. What would help is a clear, steady route into skilled work, like apprenticeships with real wages, so a young man isn't left on his own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that quiet people have fear too. I don't say much at church or at home, but I lie awake like anyone else over whether the degree I borrowed for will be worth anything.

headlineQuote: I don't say much at church or at home, but I lie awake like anyone else over whether the degree I borrowed for will be worth anything.
portrait: Zane is 24, doing a **power systems** master's after a pass in electrical engineering.
He lives at his uncle's near **Stonebridge** and helps in the family's church community.
Traditional and resistant, he never uses **AI tools** and trusts only figures he can prove.
His fallback is his father's **contracting firm** in Pine Ridge, which he sees as honest work.
Debt and **shame** about theory drive his worry, and his moods run from uneasy to alarmed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, since he is slow to change and has no room.
whatWouldHelp: A steady route into skilled work, like **apprenticeships** with real wages.
